practice.reading_en: In a fictional research methods course, Nia begins with the topic "technology and belonging." She wants to know whether digital tools improve university life, but the question includes too many tools, experiences, and student groups for a short project. Her tutor asks what evidence she could realistically examine. Nia has access to publicly shared welcome messages from two student societies and can analyze how those messages invite newcomers to participate. She revises her question to ask how the societies' welcome messages describe participation and whether they address students who cannot attend in person. This version identifies a manageable set of texts and a clear analytical focus. It does not establish whether newcomers actually feel more included; answering that would require different evidence. Nia writes this boundary into her proposal rather than hiding it. She also checks whether both societies have enough comparable messages from the same period. If one has only a single announcement, she will adjust the comparison before claiming that it represents a regular communication pattern. Narrowing the question makes the project more answerable without making the underlying issue unimportant.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word research proposal for Nia. State the focused question, identify the texts and comparison, explain feasibility, and distinguish what the analysis can and cannot establish.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以120至160詞替Nia寫研究提案，包含聚焦問題、文本與比較、可行性，以及分析能確立和不能確立之處。
practice.sample_answer_en: My project asks how two student societies' welcome messages describe participation and whether they address students who cannot attend in person. I will compare publicly shared messages from the same period, focusing on invitations, participation options, and assumptions about availability. This is more feasible than studying whether technology improves university life because it identifies a manageable set of texts and a specific analytical task. Before finalizing the comparison, I will check that both societies provide enough comparable material. A single announcement should not automatically be treated as evidence of a regular pattern. The analysis can show how participation is represented in the messages, but it cannot establish how included newcomers actually feel. I will state that limitation clearly and explain that investigating students' experiences would require additional evidence beyond the texts.

practice.reading_en: In a fictional information literacy workshop, Marco investigates how campus signs help first-time visitors find accessible routes. His first search uses the complete sentence from his research question and returns a mixture of unrelated material. The librarian asks him to separate the question into concepts: navigation, accessibility, and unfamiliar users. For each concept, Marco lists possible terms, such as wayfinding for navigation and newcomers for unfamiliar users. He notices that an article using the phrase barrier-free routes may still be relevant even if it does not use his original wording. He keeps a search log that records the terms tried, the kinds of results found, and the reason for each change. When results focus on vehicle navigation, he adds a pedestrian concept instead of assuming every irrelevant result proves the topic is unresearched. He also reads short descriptions before deciding whether a source fits the question. The workshop does not promise that a particular search system will behave in a fixed way. Marco's aim is to make his choices explainable and revisable, while recognizing that different writers may describe the same concept differently.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word search strategy for Marco. Identify three concepts, suggest alternative terms, explain one adjustment for irrelevant results, and describe what the search log should record.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以120至160詞替Marco寫搜尋策略，列三項概念及替代詞，解釋排除無關結果的調整與搜尋紀錄內容。
practice.sample_answer_en: I will organize the search around navigation, accessibility, and users who are unfamiliar with the campus. Alternative terms may include wayfinding for navigation, barrier-free routes for accessible routes, and newcomers or first-time visitors for unfamiliar users. These alternatives matter because relevant authors may not use the wording in my original question. If the results mainly discuss vehicle navigation, I will add a pedestrian concept and check whether the results become more relevant. I will read source descriptions before deciding that a text belongs in the project. My log will record the terms I tried, the kinds of results they produced, and why I changed the search. It will also note reasons for excluding sources, so I can review my decisions without treating the first unsuccessful search as proof that no useful research exists.

objectives_zh_TW: 辨認來源的目的、讀者與製作方式。

practice.reading_en: For a fictional project about a new campus garden, Leah collects three materials: an official opening announcement, a volunteer's diary, and a maintenance schedule. She initially plans to rank them from most to least trustworthy and use only the highest-ranked source. Her tutor asks what question each material can answer. The announcement explains how the institution presents the garden to the public, but it is designed to celebrate the opening rather than document every difficulty. The diary offers a detailed personal account of volunteering, yet it cannot represent all volunteers' experiences. The maintenance schedule records planned tasks, not proof that every task actually happened. Leah realizes that usefulness depends partly on the claim she wants to make. To analyze public framing, the announcement is directly relevant. To explore one volunteer's changing expectations, the diary is valuable when its perspective is identified. To compare plans with completed work, she would need records beyond the schedule. Instead of rejecting sources simply because they have a purpose or limitation, Leah states those features and chooses evidence that fits a clearly defined question.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word source-selection note for Leah. Explain what each of the three materials can support, state its limitation, and justify one choice for a focused research question.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以120至160詞替Leah寫選材筆記，說明三種材料能支持什麼及其限制，並為一個聚焦問題選擇合適來源。
practice.sample_answer_en: The opening announcement is useful for asking how the institution publicly presents the garden. Its celebratory purpose limits its value as a complete record of difficulties, but that same purpose is relevant when studying public framing. The volunteer's diary can support an analysis of one person's changing expectations; it should not stand for all volunteers. The maintenance schedule identifies planned tasks, although it cannot prove that the work was completed. For my focused question about how the garden is represented to the public, I would begin with the announcement and examine its language and selected details. I would explain its purpose rather than treat it as a neutral account of everything that happened. If I later wanted to compare plans with completed work, I would need additional records beyond the schedule.

practice.reading_en: In a fictional library evaluation exercise, a report describes a hypothetical change to an archive request form. After the form was shortened, fewer submitted requests lacked a required date. The report's author interprets this pattern as a possible sign that the revised form made the requirement easier to understand. A student reader, Chris, summarizes the report by writing that shorter forms always improve user understanding. His partner asks him to separate what was recorded from what was inferred. The recorded observation concerns missing dates in submitted requests. The explanation concerns users' understanding, which was not measured directly. The broad claim about all shorter forms goes further still. Chris returns to the report and notices that staff also began checking forms at the desk during the same period. This change could affect the number of incomplete submissions without showing that users understood the instructions better. He revises his summary to report the observed pattern and present improved understanding as one possible explanation. He also recommends gathering users' explanations of the requirement before drawing a stronger conclusion about comprehension.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word analytical note for Chris. Separate the observation, proposed interpretation, and overgeneralized claim; identify an alternative explanation and suggest evidence for a stronger understanding claim.

practice.sample_answer_en: The recorded observation is that fewer submitted archive requests lacked a required date after the form was shortened. One interpretation is that the revised form made the requirement easier to understand, but understanding was not measured directly. The statement that shorter forms always improve comprehension is therefore much broader than the evidence supports. Staff also began checking requests at the desk during the same period. Their checks could reduce incomplete submissions even if users' understanding did not change. I would revise the summary to preserve the observed pattern while presenting improved understanding as a possible explanation. To investigate that explanation more directly, we could ask users to explain the requirement in their own words. The new evidence should address comprehension rather than merely count completed fields again.

practice.reading_en: In a fictional policy-reading exercise, Rosa compares two training texts about a campus refill station. Text A recommends placing the station near the main entrance because visitors can notice it immediately. Text B favors a quieter corridor because people can refill bottles without blocking a busy doorway. Rosa first describes the texts as complete opposites. On closer reading, she sees that both support providing a refill station and both care about convenient use. Their disagreement concerns the location and the relative importance of visibility and circulation. Text A discusses how newcomers find facilities, while Text B describes the movement of groups during class changes. Neither text provides direct evidence about how many people would use each proposed location. Rosa organizes her comparison around shared aims, different criteria, and missing evidence. She concludes that the texts reveal a design tension rather than proving that one author cares about users and the other does not. A useful next step would examine whether a location can be visible without creating congestion. This question emerges from the comparison instead of merely choosing a favorite source.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word comparison of the fictional texts. Identify their shared aim, explain their different priorities and evidence, avoid a false opposition, and propose a question for further investigation.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以120至160詞比較兩篇虛構文本，指出共同目標、不同優先順序與證據，避免假對立，並提出後續問題。
practice.sample_answer_en: Both training texts support a campus refill station and aim to make it convenient to use. Their disagreement concerns location rather than the value of the facility itself. Text A prioritizes visibility near the main entrance, especially for newcomers who need to find it. Text B prioritizes circulation and warns that refilling could obstruct a busy doorway during class changes. These are different user-related criteria, so the comparison should not suggest that only one author considers users. Neither text directly establishes likely use at each proposed location. Together, they identify a tension between being easy to find and leaving enough space for movement. Further investigation could ask whether another location provides clear visibility without congestion. That question would build on both sources instead of selecting one position before examining the practical conditions.

practice.reading_en: In a fictional academic writing workshop, Eli paraphrases a short training passage about peer discussion. The passage states: "For some first-year students in this workshop, discussing an outline with a partner may help reveal unclear links between ideas." Eli's first version says that peer discussion improves all students' writing. Although he has changed the vocabulary, he has also changed the meaning. The original concerns some first-year participants in one workshop, identifies a possible benefit, and focuses on noticing unclear connections in an outline. It does not claim a general improvement in finished writing. Eli rewrites the sentence to preserve those boundaries while changing its structure. He also keeps attribution to the fictional training passage, recognizing that using his own wording does not make the underlying idea his own. To check the revision, he compares the group, activity, outcome, and degree of certainty with the original. He does not copy the entire sentence and merely replace a few words. The exercise shows that a responsible paraphrase changes expression while preserving the source's scope and evidential strength.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word paraphrase commentary. Give a faithful paraphrase of the fictional passage, explain three qualifications preserved, and state why attribution remains necessary. Treat it as training material, not a real research citation.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以120至160詞寫改寫說明，忠實改寫虛構段落、解釋三項保留限制及為何仍須註明來源；勿當真實研究引用。
practice.sample_answer_en: The fictional training passage suggests that, within this workshop, reviewing an outline with a partner could help some first-year students notice weak connections between their ideas. This paraphrase keeps the setting limited to the workshop rather than extending the finding to every learning context. It also preserves the restricted group, since the statement concerns some first-year students rather than all students. Finally, could help retains the original uncertainty and does not turn a possible benefit into a guaranteed improvement. The outcome remains noticing unclear links in an outline, not producing better finished writing in general. Attribution is still needed because the underlying idea comes from the training passage even though the wording has changed. This exercise should not be presented as evidence from a real published study. A real assignment would require suitable, verifiable sources in place of these fictional materials.

practice.reading_en: A fictional training document for a campus museum describes a proposed display as "a conversation rather than a finished answer." In a writing exercise, Sam wants to analyze how this wording presents the museum's relationship with visitors. His first paragraph ends immediately after the quotation, leaving readers to decide why it matters. He revises the paragraph by introducing the document's purpose and identifying the quoted words as the focus of his analysis. He explains that conversation suggests an exchange in which visitors may contribute, while finished answer would imply settled authority. The contrast therefore frames the display as open to interpretation. Sam also states what the quotation cannot establish: inviting participation in promotional language does not prove that visitors will actually influence display decisions. He would need evidence about the museum's practices to support that stronger claim. The quotation is clearly attributed to the fictional training document and is not presented as a real museum statement. Sam learns that an effective quotation requires a reason to preserve the exact wording and analysis that connects that wording to a limited claim.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word analytical paragraph about the fictional training quotation. Introduce its context, quote the key wording accurately, analyze the contrast, and state what the quotation cannot establish.

practice.sample_answer_en: The fictional training document presents a proposed museum display as "a conversation rather than a finished answer." This contrast matters because the two expressions assign different roles to visitors. Conversation suggests that meaning may develop through exchange, whereas a finished answer implies that the institution has already settled the issue. The wording therefore frames the display as open to interpretation and gives the reader a reason to expect participation. However, the quotation supports a claim about how the display is presented, not proof that visitors will influence actual decisions. Establishing that stronger claim would require evidence about participation practices and their effects. Preserving the exact phrase is useful here because the analysis depends on its contrasting terms. The quotation belongs to a fictional exercise and should not be cited as a real museum's statement. A real assignment would require suitable, verifiable sources in place of these fictional materials.

practice.reading_en: In a fictional methods exercise, a hypothetical survey finds that students who attended optional archive workshops report more confidence using historical sources than students who did not attend. A promotional draft says that the workshops caused the higher confidence. Amira questions this conclusion because attendance was voluntary and confidence was measured only after the sessions. Students who were already interested in archives may have been more likely to attend, and they may also have felt more confident beforehand. The survey therefore identifies an association but does not isolate the workshop's effect. Amira revises the statement to describe the observed difference without assigning a definite cause. She suggests collecting information about participants' prior experience and confidence before the workshop. Comparing changes over time would address part of the uncertainty, although it would not automatically remove every difference between the groups. She also distinguishes reported confidence from demonstrated skill; a person may feel confident without evaluating a source accurately. The exercise teaches Amira to connect the strength of the conclusion to the design of the evidence rather than to how persuasive a simple success story sounds.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word methods commentary. Report the association, explain self-selection and missing baseline evidence, distinguish confidence from skill, and propose a useful but limited improvement.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以120至160詞寫方法評析，陳述關聯，解釋自選與基準資料不足，區分信心與技能，提出有限度的改善。
practice.sample_answer_en: The hypothetical survey shows that workshop attendees reported higher confidence with historical sources than non-attendees. This is an association, not proof that the workshops caused the difference. Attendance was voluntary, so students with prior interest or experience may have been more likely to join. Confidence was measured only afterward, leaving their earlier confidence unknown. Collecting information before and after the workshop would help show whether confidence changed, and recording prior experience could clarify another difference between the groups. However, these additions would not automatically remove every alternative explanation. The outcome also needs careful naming: self-reported confidence is not the same as demonstrated source-evaluation skill. A stronger evaluation would define the intended outcome clearly and gather evidence appropriate to it, while keeping any causal conclusion proportional to the study design.

questions.prompt_en: How can voluntary attendance complicate a causal interpretation?

questions.prompt_en: Would before-and-after confidence measures prove improved source-evaluation skill? Explain.
questions.answer_en: No. They could show reported confidence changes, but skill requires appropriate performance evidence, and other differences may still complicate causation.

objectives_zh_TW: 辨識招募方式可能漏掉的群體。

practice.reading_en: In a fictional campus services exercise, an online questionnaire asks students whether they find the new appointment system easy to use. The invitation appears only inside the system, and participation is optional. Most respondents give positive answers. The project team initially writes that students are satisfied with the system. Yara asks who could have been missed. Students who could not log in would not see the invitation, while students who stopped using the system might be unlikely to respond. The sample therefore gives information about those who encountered the invitation and chose to answer, not necessarily all intended users. Adding more responses through the same route might increase the amount of information without correcting this coverage problem. Yara suggests offering another way to participate and deliberately seeking accounts from students who needed help accessing appointments. She does not claim that excluded students must be dissatisfied; their experiences are simply unknown in the current data. Her revised report preserves the positive responses while limiting the population to which they can reasonably be applied. The limitation becomes a reason for better evidence collection, not a reason to discard every response.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word sampling critique. Explain the invitation and response limits, distinguish more responses from broader coverage, avoid assuming excluded students' views, and propose an appropriate improvement.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以120至160詞評析抽樣，說明邀請與回覆限制，區分數量與涵蓋範圍，勿假設被排除者觀點，並提出改善。
practice.sample_answer_en: The questionnaire provides useful information about students who entered the appointment system, saw the invitation, and chose to respond. It may miss people who could not log in or had already stopped using the service. Positive answers therefore should not automatically be generalized to all intended users. Collecting more responses through the same invitation route would not necessarily correct the coverage gap, even if it produced a larger sample. We also should not assume that missing students are dissatisfied; the present data do not establish their views. A useful improvement would offer a separate participation route and seek experiences from students who needed help accessing appointments. The report can retain the positive findings while clearly identifying whose responses they represent and what further evidence is needed before drawing a broader conclusion.

practice.reading_en: In a fictional student research exercise, Mei examines whether a campus repair room supports independent learning. One training source summarizes booking records and reports that the room is regularly reserved. Another describes interviews in which novice users say they value staff guidance. A third presents observations of users waiting for help with unfamiliar tools. Mei's first draft summarizes each source in a separate paragraph without explaining their relationship. She reorganizes the draft around a question: what would count as evidence of independent learning? The booking records show reservations, but they do not establish actual attendance or reveal what users learn. The interviews suggest that guidance matters to novices, while the observations indicate moments when users cannot proceed alone. These findings are not necessarily contradictory. Guided participation could be part of a learning process, but none of the sources follows users long enough to show increasing independence. Mei identifies that shared gap and proposes comparing how the same users approach similar tasks over time. Her synthesis does not force every source to answer the same question equally well; it explains how different evidence contributes to a more carefully limited conclusion.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word synthesis of the three fictional training sources. Organize by the learning question, connect their different evidence, explain a shared gap, and propose a focused follow-up.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以120至160詞統整三個虛構訓練來源，以學習問題組織，連結不同證據、說明共同缺口並提出聚焦追蹤。
practice.sample_answer_en: The three training sources document reservations and the role of guidance, but they do not establish increasing independence. Booking records document reservations rather than actual attendance or learning outcomes. Interviews describe novices' appreciation of staff support, and observations show users pausing when unfamiliar tools prevent them from continuing alone. These findings can fit together: assistance may be part of learning rather than evidence that learning has failed. However, none of the sources follows the same users over time, so the materials cannot show whether dependence on help decreases with experience. A useful follow-up would examine how returning users approach similar tasks and when they seek assistance. This would address the gap more directly than collecting additional booking totals, while preserving the distinction between using a facility and developing a skill. A real assignment would require suitable, verifiable sources in place of these fictional materials.

practice.reading_en: In a fictional writing clinic, Jo drafts a paragraph using two materials labeled Training Source A and Training Source B. These documents are invented for the exercise and do not represent published research. Source A describes how a hypothetical mentoring group organizes meetings; Source B offers a participant's fictional reflection. Jo paraphrases a scheduling idea from Source A and quotes a short phrase from Source B. She initially adds realistic-looking author names and publication dates to make the paragraph appear complete. The tutor explains that these details would misrepresent the materials. Jo removes them, identifies the documents by their actual training labels, and explicitly states that they are fictional. practice.reading_en: In a fictional university writing exercise, Arjun prepares a mini literature review about peer orientation for new laboratory users. The materials are three fictional training sources, not real publications. Source A reports interviews in which newcomers describe peer explanations as approachable. Source B records observations showing that some peer guides skip safety-related steps when demonstrating familiar tasks. Source C describes a revised checklist but provides no follow-up evidence about how guides use it. Arjun initially writes one summary after another and concludes that peer orientation is effective. On revision, he organizes the review around approachability, accuracy, and the evidence needed to connect them. The interviews support a claim about newcomers' perceptions, while the observations raise a concern about consistency. The checklist is a proposed response, not demonstrated proof that the concern has been solved. Arjun identifies a gap: none of the materials establishes whether guided use of the checklist preserves approachability while improving complete demonstrations. He proposes observing that process before and after a revision, with the limits of such a comparison stated clearly. His review attributes the fictional sources accurately and keeps its conclusion narrower than the initial claim.
practice.prompt_en: Write a 120-160-word mini review of the three fictional training sources. Organize around approachability and accuracy, distinguish evidence from a proposed solution, identify a gap, and suggest a limited next step.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以120至160詞回顧三個虛構訓練來源，以親近感與準確性組織，分辨證據與提案，找出缺口並提出有限度下一步。
practice.sample_answer_en: The three fictional training sources suggest that peer orientation may be approachable, but they do not establish that it consistently provides complete demonstrations. Source A's interviews support a claim about newcomers' perceptions. Source B's observations identify omitted safety-related steps, showing why approachability alone is not enough to demonstrate overall effectiveness. Source C offers a revised checklist, but without follow-up evidence it remains a proposed response rather than a proven solution. Together, the materials reveal a gap concerning whether guided checklist use can improve completeness while preserving an approachable learning experience. Observing demonstrations before and after a revision could help investigate this question, although other changes would need consideration before making a causal claim. These sources are fictional training documents, so this review is an exercise rather than a summary of real published research. A real assignment would require suitable, verifiable sources in place of these fictional materials.
